note: Vol. II No. 18. THE RICHEST OF THE FOUR, and the issue this ticket takes the TOWN ORDINANCES from: page 1 columns 1 and 2 carry the Trustees' by-laws, passed 5 August 1835 over Hugunin's and Alex. N. Fullerton's names, and this printing sets them line by line where 12 August weaves them into two 5,000-character segmenter columns and 26 August carries only the tail. Six claims (c001-c006) hold them, and three passages in them are directly modellable: the half-sidewalk-and-two-months rule for a building site, the five-dollar penalty for riding across a bridge walk, and section 18's eighteen inches of stove pipe above every roof. Section 22's hay-stacking limit walks a six-vertex boundary through named streets and is the only documented statement in this corpus of where the built town was held to end in the scene year. Page 3 carries the month's best-placed shop (Sarah D. Howe's room in the house Dr. Austin occupies), the only numbered street address in the month (No. 1 South Water Street, near the Draw Bridge) and twenty-one named lots offered to lease. STANDING ADVERTISEMENTS unchanged from 5 August are not re-claimed here. THE LETTER LIST is the same 31 July list, printed a third time; signature claimed, names deferred to T-0336. NOT CLAIMED, AND DELIBERATELY: the 'DESTRUCTIVE FIRE' on page 3 column 1, which consumes a book store, Strickland & Gaylord's store, law offices, a looking-glass and comb factory and a coffee house for $55,000. It stands immediately under a 'Cleveland Whig, July 30' credit, the words 'of Cleveland' survive inside it, its named sufferers are not Chicago names, and no source records a fire of that size in Chicago in 1835 — it is read as an out-of-town reprint and is NOT claimed as this town's, on the same principle that quarantined the out-of-county estray notices in Vol. I No. 1. Also not claimed: pages 1-2 national politics and the Ottawa probate notices.

claims.notes: THE TOWN GOVERNS ITS OWN STREET WIDTH, AND THE NUMBERS ARE MODELLABLE. Three of them: building materials may not be left in a street at all without leave; a builder MAY occupy the street beside his own lot, but not more than one half of the sidewalk nor of the carriage way, and for no longer than two months; and goods may stand on the sidewalk in front of a store no farther than four feet into it. That is a rule for what a Chicago street looked like in August 1835 — timber and brick piled against half a footway, boxes standing four feet out from a shop front, and both of them ordinary enough to be legislated for. The column is the worst-cut matter this ticket claims, two physical columns woven line by line, so almost every clause carries a supply; the sections are numbered in the printed ordinance and the numbers are among the things the column lost. The 12 August issue prints the same forme in a shape a quote cannot be built from at all.

Section 18 says, in August 1835 and under a five-dollar penalty, that every stove pipe or chimney passing through a roof SHALL BE CARRIED AT LEAST EIGHTEEN INCHES ABOVE IT; that no stove pipe may go out through a side or end wall at all; and that where a pipe passes a wooden or lath-and-plaster partition it must be sleeved in a stone or earthen cylinder, surrounded by brick, or run through a tin or sheet-iron plate held a quarter inch clear, with three inches clear of any woodwork. A roof line in this reconstruction that carries stub pipes, or pipes out through a gable end, is contradicted by the town's own by-law. Sections 15 to 17 are the same fear from the other side: shavings swept out of a shop once a week, no bonfires in a street or on a lot without leave. claims.notes: A HAY-STACKING BOUNDARY WALKED STREET BY STREET, AND IT IS A POLYGON. Washington street at the United States Reservation, west to Canal Street, north to Kinzie Street, east to Wolcott street, thence to Illinois Street, and thence to Lake Michigan — six vertices, all of them named streets this reconstruction already carries, describing the ground the Trustees thought dense enough that a hay stack in it was a fire risk. It is the only documented statement in the corpus of where the BUILT town was held to end in the scene year, and it is drawn from the fort's reservation round the forks and back to the lake. Section 21 is its companion: a fire warden per district walking into every house, store and shop nine months of the year, checking the chimneys, ovens, stoves, pipes, hearths, boilers and wash houses that section 18 regulates. Passed 5 August 1835 over the names of the President, Hugunin, and the Secretary, Alexander N. Fullerton. The section 22 preamble is read from the 12 and 26 August printings, which set it whole where this column jumps from 'unsafe' to 'North to the intersection'.

Grand River, St. Joseph, Milwaukee, Oswego, Detroit and Buffalo — the lake trade Chicago lived on, at a rate of better than one vessel a day, each with its master named. A vessel list is therefore not decoration here — it is the traffic those piers were built to take.

Either a two-man partnership became one man inside three weeks, or two tailors' shops stood within a few doors of each other opposite the same coffee house. The papers of August do not decide it and neither does this claim; the two names are NOT merged, because same surname with a different spelling is exactly the judgement identity.json exists to make explicitly. claims.notes: THE 31 JULY 1835 POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST, MINTED ONCE AND FROM THIS PRINTING (T-0336). One list, four printings: the same standing forme was pulled in the Democrats of 5, 12, 19 and 26 August 1835, and its heading — legible only in the 26 August setting — dates it to the 31st day of July 1835 over John S. C. Hogan, P. M. THE NAMES ARE MINTED HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE. T-0299 measured the alternative: 298 names minted from three printings of the 1834 list became 638 persons, because the identity policy keys on the whole normalized name and each printing's OCR segments it differently. The other three printings carry a claim naming this list and minting no names at all — 08-05 c027 and 08-26 c008 quote the heading, 08-12 c014 and 08-19 c019 the signature. WHY THE 19 AUGUST PRINTING. All four settings are the same type, and all four were OCR'd with the low-agreement warning the transcription carries at the head of every column here. Read against each other, this one holds the most of the list in continuous readable type: its column 2 sets 281 names in one line of 5,081 characters and its column 3 sets the rest across nine lines with no advertising woven through them, where the 12 and 26 August settings break their first column mid-run and the 5 August setting loses most of its second. TWO WITNESSES, AND IT IS SAID HERE. Four OCR readings of one forme mean a letter lost in this printing is often clean in another, and the 26 and 12 August settings were read beside this one to resolve letters. EVERY letter taken from them is bracketed in `normalized` and the `as_printed` beside it is this printing's own characters, unaltered — a supply is visible or it is a smoothing. Nothing was resolved from a printing into a name this one does not set: where the type here is gone, the reading carries `[...]` and the entity stands as printed rather than being filled in from a neighbour. WHAT IS NOT CORRECTED. A name whose initial is present but disagrees with its section is a MISREADING and stands as printed (`Rentley, A inson` under B, `Poser, eb` under F); only `identity.json` may say two spellings are one person, and only with a merge_rule naming both. Where a name begins in lower case its capital was cut by the column edge and the section letter is supplied in brackets, the same rule the 1 July read used. THIS CLAIM IS THE FIRST OF THE LIST'S TWO PRINTED COLUMNS, issue page 4 column 2 — 281 names, the surnames A to F in its left sub-column and G to P in its right. The transcription wove the two sub-columns together line by line, alternating left name and right name, which is why one line of the text carries the whole column; the entities are given in the PAGE's order (the left run down, then the right run down) and not in the quote's woven order, because an alphabetical run is only legible unwoven. The quote is the woven line, verbatim, from the first name to the column's end; the heading above it is quoted at 08-05 c027 and 08-26 c008 and is not re-quoted here. ONE ENTRY IS LEFT UNJOINED ON PURPOSE: `Clark Darlus or G. P` is followed, in this printing and in the 26 August one alike, by `Post.` standing alone on the next line of the same sub-column, which reads as the tail of that entry — 'Clark, Darius or G. P. Post'. Both are recorded as they stand, because joining them would be a guess and the two printings agree only about the line break.
